findings.title: Neighbor query and BulkForce contracts force per-agent Python loops, contradicting the slice's own hot-path requirement and the architecture's GPU-compatibility goal
findings.description:
- Step 3 of the Data Flow (line 88) says "For each *active* agent, `SpatialQuery.query_radius(position, radius)`". The protocol at lines 165-167 takes one position and returns a variable-length index array.
- `BulkForce` therefore receives `neighbor_lists: list[NDArray[np.intp]]` (line 145), which is a ragged Python list built one agent at a time. It also receives `profiles: list[BehavioralProfile]` (line 146), so each force has to look up profile fields agent by agent.
- This contradicts the slice's Technical Requirement at line 247: "No Python-level per-agent loops in the hot path".
- It also contradicts the architecture at `100-arch.behavior-engine.md:99`, which calls for "bulk array-in/array-out operations with no Python-level per-agent branching, no dynamic allocation". Lists of per-agent arrays are dynamic allocation every tick.
- It weakens the "Pluggable spatial queries" principle (`100-arch...md:45`). A spatial hash for slice 105, or a GPU index, cannot answer a batch query through a per-point interface, so swapping one in would require changing the engine.
- **Fix:**
  - Add a bulk query, e.g. `query_radius_batch(indices, radii)`, that returns a flat CSR-style result (`offsets`, `neighbor_indices`).
  - Pass profile parameters to forces as per-agent arrays, gathered once per tick through `profile_indices`, instead of a list of dataclasses.
  - Lock this in now, because slices 101-105 all build on these signatures.

findings.title: Brute-force `build()` precomputes an O(n²) pairwise matrix that `query_radius(position, …)` cannot use
findings.description:
- Line 173 says the brute-force implementation "computes all pairwise distances on `build()` and filters by radius on `query_radius()`".
- `query_radius` takes an arbitrary `position`, not an agent index. A matrix of agent-to-agent distances cannot answer it without first mapping the position back to an agent, so each query still costs O(n) distance math.
- The precomputation is therefore wasted O(n²) time and memory: about 800 MB of float64 at 10K agents, which is the scale the architecture targets.
- **Fix (lighter):** `build()` stores the positions and `query_radius` computes distances on demand. Alternatively, if the bulk query from the previous finding is adopted, the batch query can compute distances in one vectorized pass.

findings.title: Architecture scale NFR not restated
findings.description:
- The architecture states an NFR for the tick path: "Support tens of thousands of agents at full behavioral fidelity on a single CPU process" (`100-arch.behavior-engine.md:33`).
- This slice creates that tick path but only mentions "the hundreds-of-agents scale this slice targets" (line 173). It does not restate the architecture target or say which slice must meet it.
- **Fix:**
  - Restate the NFR with its target.
  - State the target this slice must meet (e.g. N agents per tick within T ms with brute force).
  - Say explicitly that meeting the tens-of-thousands target is deferred to slice 105.

findings.title: Per-agent `Force` protocol and `accelerations` array have no consumer, so cut them
findings.description:
**`Force` protocol:**
- `tick()` accepts only `forces: list[BulkForce]` (line 185).
- Yet line 152 says "The tick loop prefers the bulk variant when available", and line 248 requires placeholders to "exercise both the `Force` and `BulkForce` protocol paths".
- There is no per-agent path in `tick`, and no adapter is specified. Either the tick needs undocumented type dispatch (an OCP violation) or the `Force` protocol is dead code.
- The architecture (`100-arch...md:99`) points only at the bulk pattern.
- **Fix:** cut `Force` and line 248. A reference implementation for tests can be a test helper.

**`accelerations` array:**
- `accelerations` (N×2, line 96) is never read or written by the data flow. Integration goes straight from force to velocity (line 90).
- **Fix:** cut it until a slice needs it.

findings.title: Inconsistent return contract against the architecture's envisioned tick
findings.description:
- Line 39 says the tick should "return updated state".
- The signature returns `None` and mutates in place (lines 187, 191, 91).
- The architecture describes "Returns the updated state array" and "feed in state, get back state" (`100-arch...md:68-70`).
- In-place mutation is a reasonable performance choice, but the world server depends on this contract. That matters for replay snapshots, and for double-buffering if the world server reads state while ticking.
- **Fix:** state the in-place contract as a deliberate deviation from the architecture, with the reason, and make line 39 match it.

findings.title: Input validation and boundary semantics under-specified for `active_indices`, removal and neighbor results
findings.description:
**`active_indices` (line 186):**
- The slice says nothing about out-of-range values, duplicates or dtype.
- With `state.velocities[active_indices] += …` (line 215), duplicate indices are silently applied once. That breaks the "only these agents, correctly" contract, and nothing makes the failure visible.

**`profile_indices`:**
- An index past `len(profiles)` is not covered.
- **Fix:** define fail-fast checks at the `tick()` boundary for both, in line with the "Fail Fast" and "no silent fallback" project rules.

**Agent removal:**
- The architecture's narrow interface includes "register/remove agents" (`100-arch...md:81`), but the slice does not define removal semantics (compaction vs swap-remove).
- Either way, removal changes agent indices that the world server and `active_indices` callers hold.
- **Fix:** state the index-stability contract.

**Neighbor results:**
- The slice does not say whether `query_radius` includes the querying agent itself.
- Slice 101's separation and cohesion forces depend on this.
- **Fix:** specify it.

findings.title: Determinism walkthrough depends on unspecified initial-state generation
findings.description:
- The determinism check at lines 274-283 compares two independent `AgentState.create(n=100, …)` calls, but the slice does not say how `create` sets initial positions and velocities.
- If `create` randomizes them without a seed, the check fails. If everything starts at the origin with no force, the check passes trivially.
- The subset check at line 290 ("agent 50 nearby agent 0") also needs explicit placement.
- **Fix:** state that `create` is deterministic (zeros or an explicit seed parameter).

findings.title: Integration section is indented as a code block
findings.description:
- Lines 205-215 are indented four spaces, so Markdown renders the "Integration: Semi-Implicit Euler" heading and its text as a code block.
- **Fix:** remove the indentation.

findings.title: Scope matches slice plan entry and dependency direction is correct
findings.description:
- Every item in the slice plan's (100) entry is included: project structure, SoA state, profile, subset-evaluable tick, semi-implicit Euler, spatial interface with brute force, and deterministic output.
- The exclusions match the plan: specific forces go to 101, inter-profile rules to 103, the spatial hash to 105, and serialization to the world server.
- `spatial/` depends only on NumPy types, and `engine/` depends on the `SpatialQuery` protocol, so the dependency points inward.
- The subset-evaluable tick builds the spatial index from the full population, which matches the architecture's principle at `100-arch...md:49` and its considerations at `100-arch...md:97`.
- Keeping float64 internally and leaving conversion to the serialization boundary matches `100-arch...md:95`.
